title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
gist: A late-September Trump executive order directs federal agencies to rebrand AI as "Super Intelligence" (SI); one month in, adoption is patchy across agencies, media and Big Tech, with only Zuckerberg and Musk using it consistently on Q3 earnings calls. The author warns the rebrand risks turning AI terminology into a partisan loyalty test just as AI becomes a top midterm election issue.

insights.claim: At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with a single directive ordering government agencies to rebrand artificial intelligence as 'Super Intelligence', a term chosen over 'Extreme Intelligence' and 'Supreme Intelligence' in a poll on X.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Signals the administration is using AI branding as a political instrument, which can affect vendor messaging in government contracting.

insights.claim: The stated rationale for the rename is that today's AI systems 'amplify human ingenuity' rather than merely 'imitate' intelligence.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Reflects an administration framing of AI as powerful and pro-growth, consistent with a permissive policy stance.
insights.locator: The stated reason for this name

insights.claim: Under the order, federal agency leaders must draft a new legislative definition of 'Super Intelligence' for the president by the end of the month, though the order does not apply to previously issued regulations or documents.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A legal definition of 'Super Intelligence' could shape future regulation and procurement scope.

insights.claim: Trump suggested a new rule may go further than the executive order and outright ban 'artificial intelligence' from government documents.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Escalation would raise compliance and relabeling pressure for government contractors.
insights.locator: In the past couple of weeks

insights.claim: 'SI' is appearing more often in government solicitations, including an ICE request for companies to build 'SI-powered' surveillance for detention facilities.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Government procurement language is shifting, so contractors bidding on federal AI work may need to adopt the new terminology.

insights.claim: Adoption across government is inconsistent: the Pentagon's Project Meridian used the old terminology, an FTC release used 'superintelligence', HHS releases show no new language, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said 'AI' in an October 3 interview.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Patchy compliance suggests the rebrand is largely symbolic for now, with limited practical policy effect.

insights.claim: The term 'AI' will likely persist given the many AI-named offices and programs created in recent years, such as the Pentagon's Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
entities: Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office
insights.so_what: Institutional inertia limits how far the rebrand can reshape government AI programs.

insights.claim: Pichai, Amodei, Zuckerberg, Brockman, Musk and Huang signed the nonbinding White House Accord on Super Intelligence released the same day as the rebrand order.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
entities: White House Accord on Super Intelligence
insights.so_what: Top AI leaders are publicly aligning with the White House on a voluntary safety framework, signaling a cooperative, light-touch regulatory posture.

insights.claim: A CNBC analysis of third-quarter earnings calls found only Zuckerberg and Musk used 'Super Intelligence' consistently, and Meta had already been saying 'superintelligence' since the previous year.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Corporate language is a cheap signal of political alignment; most firms are hedging rather than fully conforming.

insights.claim: Musk's companies use the term the most and he pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, though he still mixes SI and AI on X.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Musk-linked companies are positioning most visibly with the administration, which may matter for government contracts.

insights.claim: Executives from Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet used 'AI' on their earnings calls, though Microsoft's recent shareholder letter referred to the 'Super Intelligence era', and Huang uses both terms.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Large caps are straddling, avoiding a clear political stance in investor communications.

insights.claim: Based on past rebrands such as the Gulf of America, the author argues the 'Super Intelligence' term will become a political loyalty test, noting the administration barred the Associated Press from some events for not adopting 'Gulf of America'.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Companies and media face reputational and access risk depending on the vocabulary they adopt.
insights.quote: It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test
insights.locator: It will turn a choice of words

insights.claim: On October 27 Trump criticized the Wall Street Journal on Truth Social for not using 'Super Intelligence', yet even pro-Trump outlet Newsmax is not using the preferred term.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Limited uptake even among friendly media suggests the term may not stick outside government.
insights.quote: the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.
insights.locator: In the past couple of weeks

insights.claim: The AI rebrand may be the boldest yet because two-thirds of Americans report interacting with AI multiple times a week, unlike obscure geographic renamings.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Mass AI usage makes AI terminology and policy a high-salience consumer and political issue.

themes.theme: AI as a depolarized but rising election issue

insights.claim: The author argues public views on AI, including outright hostility, do not yet map onto partisan divisions, but a terminology loyalty test risks polarizing the AI conversation like immigration or climate change.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Polarization of AI could make AI regulation swing with election cycles, increasing policy uncertainty for the sector.
insights.quote: those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions

insights.claim: Americans say AI is more important to them in the midterm elections than environmental and climate policy, and Democrats rank it above abortion and gun policy.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: High voter salience raises the odds of AI-focused legislation and political scrutiny of AI companies.

insights.claim: Public conversations about AI the author overhears most often focus on a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare, alongside a widespread desire to have a say in how the technology transforms people's lives.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Job-loss and military fears are the dominant public narratives that could drive backlash and regulation.
